title: Family stories
summary: Soldiers, sea voyages, Czech villages, the work our people did, and the famous cousins we share ancestors with. Every story here comes from a real record or a published book; anything not yet proven is marked family claim or possible.

sections.heading: Military

entries.title: Philip Wood, Private, Revolutionary War
entries.detail: Marched from Rehoboth to Bristol, R.I., on the alarm of 8 Dec 1776, Capt. Stephen Bullock's company, Col. Thomas Carpenter's regiment, 16 days. Source: Massachusetts Soldiers and Sailors of the Revolutionary War, vol. 17, p. 766 (1908), archive.org/details/masssoldiers17bostrich; also Cabot, Annals of Brattleboro 1:159.

entries.title: A Philip Wood listed as deserted, Slade's Ferry
entries.detail: Same book, same page. Nothing shows this is our Philip; it may be another man.

entries.title: Col. Timothy Church, Vermont officer
entries.detail: A real Revolutionary officer of Brattleboro. That he is our Abigail Church's family is not yet proven (Cabot, Annals of Brattleboro).

entries.detail: Registered 5 Jun 1917, Milwaukee: 695 12th St, welder at Harley-Davidson, had declared intention to become a citizen, born Mahren (Moravia). Source: U.S. WWI Draft Registration Cards (NARA M1509), as read in our research files.

sections.heading: Ships & Arrivals
rows: Passenger list image; arrival cert. 1072798 in his naturalization papers
after: Peter came over alone at 20. On the ship list he named his mother Veronika back home in Košťany, Bohemia, and said his father Jan was already in America. He was going to Milwaukee. His naturalization petition (No. 855, Manitowoc, granted 6 Jun 1922) repeats the ship and date.
Careful: another young Petr Konečný landed at Galveston on the Rhein in Dec 1912. He was a miner bound for Texas and is not our Peter.

Howland's fall overboard: during a fierce storm mid-ocean, John Howland fell into the sea. He grabbed a topsail halyard trailing in the water and was hauled back aboard. Governor William Bradford told the story in Of Plymouth Plantation; it is retold at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Howland.

Without that rope there would be no Howland line, and no us on this side. Elizabeth Tilley was a teenager on the same ship and lost both parents that first winter. Read more at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Howland and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Tilley.

Anna Tauber's arrival: not found yet. She was born in Mostiště (written 'Moštice' in the Radnice parish register) near Radnice, Bohemia, on 15 Sep 1891 and married Peter in Chicago on 22 Feb 1919, so she arrived before then. Source: SOA Plzeň (Porta fontium), Radnice parish register RO 32, births 1883–1909, p. 96, https://www.portafontium.eu/iipimage/30071489/radnice-ro-32_0901-n.

places.heading: Svatý Štěpán (Bylnice): Peter's birthplace
paragraphs: A glassworks hamlet founded after 1815 by Count Štěpán Illésházy, owner of the Brumov estate, and named for him. The houses were workers' homes around the glass furnace, which ran until the Depression shut it in 1936. Peter Petr Pavel was born here at house 160 on 28 Jun 1893 and baptized the next day in Brumov parish. Its chapel is St. John of Nepomuk, built after 1815; the parish church is St. Wenceslas in Brumov, from the 1300s.
Birth record: MZA Brno, Acta Publica book 4021, image 151, mza.cz/actapublica/matrika/detail/300. Map: openstreetmap.org/?mlat=49.0453&mlon=18.0289#map=14/49.0453/18.0289
places.alt: Svatý Štěpán, místní část města Brumov-Bylnice
places.credit: Photo: Zvonicek, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

places.heading: Bylnice
paragraphs: First written mention 1422. Today the southern part of the town of Brumov-Bylnice, in the White Carpathians near the Slovak border. Source: cs.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bylnice. Map: openstreetmap.org/?mlat=49.0769&mlon=18.0192#map=14/49.0769/18.0192
places.credit: Photo: Pavel Hrdlička, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

places.heading: Štítná nad Vláří
paragraphs: First mentioned in 1374, in the Vlára river valley. Its parish church of St. Joseph is a classical-style building, protected as a monument since 1958. Grandfather Jan married here and worked at the manor farm. Source: cs.wikipedia.org/wiki/Štítná_nad_Vláří-Popov. Map: openstreetmap.org/?mlat=49.0695&mlon=17.9753#map=14/49.0695/17.9753
places.credit: Photo: Palickap, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

places.heading: Vlachovice
paragraphs: A village on the little Vlára river, about 5 km from Valašské Klobouky. Parish church of St. Michael the Archangel. Great-great-grandfather Pavel Konečný worked at the manor farm here. Source: cs.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vlachovice_(okres_Zlín). Map: openstreetmap.org/?mlat=49.1238&mlon=17.9400#map=14/49.1238/17.9400
places.credit: Photo: Palickap, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

places.heading: Lidečko
paragraphs: First mentioned in 1424, in the Senice valley. Church of St. Catherine of Alexandria, built about 1700 on the site of a 1511 church destroyed in Tatar raids in the 1600s. Home of Marina Trchel, Pavel's wife. Source: cs.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lidečko. Map: openstreetmap.org/?mlat=49.2030&mlon=18.0513#map=14/49.2030/18.0513
places.credit: Photo: palickap, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

places.heading: Hluk
paragraphs: A small town first mentioned in 1294, near Uherské Hradiště, known for its old fortress (tvrz) and folk traditions. Parish church of St. Lawrence. Peter's birth record calls his grandfather Jan a servant at the lord's farm in Hluk. Source: cs.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hluk_(okres_Uherské_Hradiště). Map: openstreetmap.org/?mlat=48.9881&mlon=17.5267#map=14/48.9881/17.5267
places.credit: Photo: Rios, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

places.heading: Mostiště (written 'Moštice' in the register)
paragraphs: A small village near Radnice in Bohemia, now part of Hlohovice in the Rokycany district, about 2 km southwest of Hlohovice. First written mention 1363. Anna (Tauber) Konecny was born here on 15 Sep 1891. Source: cs.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mostiště_(Hlohovice). Birth record: SOA Plzeň, Radnice RO 32 p. 96, https://www.portafontium.eu/iipimage/30071489/radnice-ro-32_0901-n. Map: openstreetmap.org/?mlat=49.8761&mlon=13.6306#map=14/49.8761/13.6306
places.credit: Photo: Pavel Hrdlička, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sections.heading: What They Did for a Living
rows: Glazier (1913), glass blower (1915), welder at Harley-Davidson (1917), welder in Manitowoc (1921)
Ship list, declaration 10633, draft card, petition 855
Day laborer (1893), glassworks helper (1895), Svatý Štěpán
Servant at the lord's manor farm (Hluk; Štítná at his wedding)
Manor farm servant at Vlachovice (named as dead at son's wedding)
Oath commissioner (14 Jan 1838, Shefford); Justice of the Peace (20 Dec 1838, Farnham)
Landowner who opened a street in Granby (1860)
SHHY, La toponymie de Granby, shhy.info
after: Life at the glassworks: whole families lived in company houses beside the furnace. Men worked in heat and smoke making window and table glass, and boys started young as helpers. Peter grew up in that trade, so it makes sense he arrived as a glazier and later welded.

Life as a manor servant: under the old estate system, landless men worked the lord's farm for wages and keep. A cottager owned a small house but little land, and a pasekář farmed steep cleared hillsides. It was a hard, poor life, and a big reason so many young people left for America.

The phrase herrschaftlicher Knecht (lord's farmhand) for Pavel is a family claim from the German-language summary; the Czech wedding record says služebný v panském dvoře, which means the same thing. His own marriage to Marina Trchel has not been found.

callout.text: We are not descended from these people. We share an ancestor with them, often 10 to 14 generations back, which makes them very distant cousins.

groups.label: Our line
groups.value: Their daughter Hope Howland m. John Chipman, then down to Hannah Nelson, who m. Jabez Wood in 1720, then the Woods to Marjorie June Wood, Frank's wife

groups.value: Alice Freeman Thompson Parke (about 1595–1664), Connecticut, a proven royal-descent gateway

groups.label: Our line
groups.value: Parke, Larrabee, Safford, Whipple, Church, Wood. One step (Elizabeth Whipple to Abigail Church) rests on a compiled source only, so this cousinship is possible, not proven.
